prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

More than a hundred dollars of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass things to stuff them in. Now a white and purple cloud is breathing in each corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table— each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I watch children shuffle strictly in line, cradle candles that dribbled hot white on their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad? Didn't I use to go mucking through streambeds with the skunk cabbage raising bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies and smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights have to be not switched on. And in close darkness the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does. I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring and one tall room and the tremble of my phone. I'm not the only one that love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being ripped to prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun I feel I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.

outputs.L3:
On impulse, I spent more than a hundred dollars on flowers today. It was reckless, perhaps, but I could not help myself. Now my beloved room brims with them—blooms spilling from every vase, tumbling in bright profusion across the dining table until the whole space feels transformed, saturated with color and life.

Surrounded by such abundance, I find old memories rising unbidden. I remember watching children in the Easter processions of Sevilla, their solemn faces caught in flickering candlelight. I remember wandering through the muddy streambeds of some half-forgotten spring, where skunk cabbage thrust its violet spears up through the cold earth. These recollections arrive together, carrying a strange and tender mixture of sorrow and wonder, as though grief and awe were never truly separate things.

As the afternoon dissolves into night, the lilies begin to assert themselves. Their fragrance, sweet beyond bearing, deepens and thickens in the darkening air until it seems almost violent in its intensity—so overwhelming that I feel it could cut me open, split me down to something raw and unguarded.

And in that moment I understand that I am not alone in this. I am not the only one whose life feels so contingent, so precariously balanced—hung upon the fragile scaffolding of a single season, a single room, the desperate hope that a phone might tremble with word from someone I love. So many of us live this way, tethered to small and breakable things.

This is what love does. It leaves me torn apart and yet somehow lightened, exposed to the open air and strangely weightless. I think of bedsheets shredded into prayer flags, fluttering their supplications to the wind. I think of a fall that has lasted for decades—a long, headfirst plunge through empty space, with no ground yet in sight.
outputs.L4:
# On Lilies and Transparency

I spent over a hundred dollars on lilies today—an absurd sum, I know, the kind of extravagance you can't justify to anyone, least of all yourself. But there I stood at the counter, watching the florist wrap them, stem after stem after stem, and I understood that this was not really about flowers at all.

I brought them home and arranged them slowly, deliberately, filling every vase I owned and then some, until the whole apartment brimmed with white. And then their scent arrived—that heavy, insistent perfume that doesn't ask permission. It filled the rooms and filled my chest, and suddenly I was undone by it, opened like a door left carelessly ajar.

Because that is what love does. It comes in through the senses—a fragrance, a color, the particular way the light falls across a petal—and before you can defend yourself, it has summoned everything: the memories you thought you'd folded neatly away, the longing that never truly left, the tender ache of wanting someone who is not here.

I stood among all that whiteness and felt myself becoming *transparent*. Not invisible—the opposite. I mean that love had made me clear as glass, and anyone might look straight through me and see the trembling machinery of my wanting. There is a particular terror in this, in being so completely exposed, in having no wall left to hide behind.

And yet—and this is the strange gift of it—I also felt weightless. As though love, in stripping me bare, had also freed me from something. The exposure and the liberation were the same sensation, indistinguishable, painful and glorious at once.

This, I think, is love's oldest secret, the thing it does to everyone who has ever surrendered to it: it makes your whole life feel *conditional*. Suddenly nothing is settled, nothing is certain. Your entire existence hangs suspended, held in a breathless pause, tremulously waiting—for a footstep in the hall, a voice on the phone, a hand reaching toward yours across the impossible distance.

I bought a hundred dollars' worth of lilies. And they taught me that I am still capable of being this open, this ruined, this alive—still waiting, always waiting, for the connection that would make me whole.
outputs.L5:
# More Than I Knew Then

There was a time when I believed that having **more** would finally make me happy. More money, more possessions, more recognition from the people around me. I chased after these things without stopping to ask whether they were truly what I needed.

Looking back, I **didn't** understand what I was missing. I **didn't** realize that the constant pursuit of *more* was quietly stealing my present moments away from me. Every time I reached one goal, another appeared on the horizon, and I told myself that satisfaction was always just a little further ahead.

But **now**, things feel different. **Now**, I try to notice the small things: the warmth of morning light, a genuine conversation, the quiet comfort of a familiar routine. I've come to learn that contentment rarely comes from adding **more** to our lives. More often, it comes from appreciating what is already here.

I **didn't** arrive at this understanding overnight. It took mistakes, disappointments, and time to see that the richest moments often ask nothing extra of us. They simply ask us to be present.

So if I could share one lesson, it would be this: don't wait for **more** to start living. Don't assume that happiness lies somewhere in the future. Begin **now**, exactly where you are, with exactly what you have. You may discover, as I did, that it was enough all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about impulsively buying too many flowers and the overwhelming, almost painful beauty of lilies filling a room at dusk, weaving in memories and a sense of vulnerability in love.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Lilies

I bought too many. I know this now, standing in the doorway as evening pours itself thin and gold across the floorboards—armfuls of them, white and impossible, more than any single room should hold, more than any single heart should risk.

The woman at the market smiled when I couldn't stop. *Just one more bunch,* I said, and then another, until my arms were full of trembling stems and my wallet emptied like a confession. I couldn't help it. There is a hunger in me that wants beauty in excess, that wants to drown in the very thing that undoes me.

Now they open in the dusk-light, these lilies, unfurling their throats like they're about to sing or scream, and the scent—God, the scent—it fills the room until the air grows heavy as memory. It presses against my chest the way your hand once did, that first night, when I understood that loving you would cost me something I hadn't yet learned to name.

Lilies smell like funerals and weddings both. Like the beginning and the ending folded into the same white petal. My grandmother kept them by her bed those last weeks, and I remember thinking beauty could be cruel, how it insists on blooming even as we're leaving.

Here is what I know: to fill a room with lilies is to admit you are not safe. Their perfume is too much, their whiteness too pure, their brief lives too tender against the coming dark. I have made myself defenseless in this small apartment, surrounded by the very thing that will wilt by week's end, that already carries its dying in its opening.

Isn't that love, though? This deliberate, foolish gathering of what cannot last?

The dusk deepens. The lilies glow like small moons in the gathering shadow, and I sit among them, unbearably open, thinking of you, thinking of everything I've ever loved too much and too helplessly—

and I would buy them all again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person prose poem in the style of a contemporary confessional poet, exploring extravagance, memory, spring, longing, and the intoxicating scent of lilies at nightfall.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nocturne with Lilies and Everything I Couldn't Keep

Tonight the lilies open like a confession I keep rehearsing—their throats thrown back, obscene with wanting, and I am the fool who planted them, who paid too much, who always pays too much for beauty that insists on dying.

Let me be honest: I have never known restraint. I bought the whole armful, the excess of them, white as the dresses I wore before I understood what white was supposed to promise. Spring makes a spendthrift of me. Everything budding at once, the world overdrawn on green, and I want to press my face against all of it, to swallow the season whole.

The scent arrives at nightfall like a debt collector for the heart. This is when memory comes—not gently, never gently—but the way perfume enters a room before the woman does. And suddenly I am seventeen again, or thirty, or some age that no longer has a number, only a temperature, only the particular dark of a particular garden where I first learned that longing has a fragrance, that it smells exactly like this: sweet enough to sicken, sweet enough to summon everyone I've lost to stand just out of reach among the stems.

I am telling you I have wasted so much. Whole years I let ripen and rot on the branch. Loves I spent like a woman who believed the coffers were bottomless. And still—*still*—I would do it all again, would empty myself extravagantly, because what is a life that hoards itself? What good is a lily that refuses to unfist its own gold?

The nightfall thickens. The lilies pour themselves out into the dark, unashamed, and I stand here breathing them, intoxicated, ruined, alive—my whole reckless inheritance of memory rising like scent, like spring, like the last luxurious spending of the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece that captures the feeling of being consumed by love and the senses—use flowers, the fading afternoon light, religious memory, and imagery of prayer flags and transparency.
counterfactuals.output:
# Litany for the Fading Hour

There is a way the light goes soft at four o'clock
that makes me think of you—the way it thins
against the wall like something almost sacred,
the way it asks for nothing and takes everything.

I am undone by peonies today.
They open past their prime, blowsy and generous,
petals loosening the way I loosen
when your hand finds the small of my back,
when the afternoon dissolves us both
into a warmth we cannot name.

*Remember the incense?*
Remember kneeling as a child, the wafer
dissolving on the tongue, that first knowledge
that the body could become a door?
I did not understand then what the nuns meant
by *transubstantiation*—how a thing
could stay itself and become something more.
Now I know. Now I feel it in my hands
each time I hold your face like communion.

Prayer flags fray on the balcony,
their colors bleeding into wind and weather.
This is the theology I trust:
that love, like cloth, is meant to thin,
to give its brightness back to the air,
to become translucent, then transparent,
until you can see straight through it
to the sky that was always waiting there.

I am translucent now.
Hold me to the window and the light
comes through the veins of me,
through peony and prayer and the memory
of every altar I have ever knelt before.

The afternoon is almost gone.
Let it go. Let me be consumed—
petal, flag, and fading gold—
until there is nothing left of me
but the scent of what we were,
hanging in the darkening room
like the ghost of some devotion
neither of us will ever quite outgrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an emotional, sensory prose poem about a person who spent over a hundred dollars on flowers, describing the room filling with fragrance and darkness while reflecting on their emotional fragility.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Wilting Light

I spent everything on you—
petals, I mean, the hundred-dollar dream of them,
peonies fat as fists uncurling,
ranunculus wound tight as the things I cannot say.

The clerk wrapped them in paper
and I carried them home like a wound I chose,
like proof that I could still make beauty
happen with my hands, with money,
with the desperate arithmetic of the lonely.

Now they open in the dark.

The room fills first with scent—
that green and dizzy sweetness,
the way lilies exhale their heavy perfume
until the air grows thick as grief,
until I am breathing them
and they are breathing me,
and I cannot tell where the fragrance ends
and my own trembling begins.

Dusk comes in blue and lowers itself
over the vase, the table, the trembling
architecture of my ribs.
I sit in the deepening dark
and let the flowers become shadows,
let their colors drain into the room's slow bruise,
and I think: *how easily I break.*

How a stem bends.
How a bloom, at its most open,
is also at its most ready to fall.

I spent everything.
I always do—
pouring myself out like water into cut glass,
hoping something rooted might drink,
might last,
might tell me I was worth the wilting.

The petals will brown at the edges by Thursday.
I know this. I bought them anyway.
Because sometimes the only prayer I have
is to fill a dark room with dying things
and call it love,
and call it enough,
and sit here breathing
while the sweetness overwhelms me,
soft and total,
like the tenderness
I keep forgetting
to give myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
